title: The Dunning–Kruger effect is messier than you think
summary: A famous 1999 study found low performers overestimated their skill. Later work shows part of that pattern can come from statistics alone — the clearer lesson is that most of us judge ourselves poorly.
evidenceNote: The original pattern shows up reliably in data, but researchers disagree about how much reflects a real psychological effect versus statistical artefacts such as regression to the mean.

scenes.text: "The less people know, the more confident they are." You've heard it. Is it true?
In the 1999 study, people who scored around the 12th percentile guessed they were near the 62nd.

left.label: Low scorers
left.text: Overestimated their rank by a lot

scenes.text: So is it a real effect of ignorance?
scenes.answer: It's debated. Similar patterns can appear from statistics alone, such as regression to the mean.

scenes.text: The safest lesson: we all misjudge our own skill. Seek real feedback.

sources.title: Unskilled and unaware of it: how difficulties in recognizing one's own incompetence lead to inflated self-assessments
sources.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Kruger & Dunning)

sources.title: The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact
